Applications in gynecological cancer drug delivery Targeted drug delivery systems The design of targeted drug delivery systems focus on enhancing the precision and efficacy of cancer treatment by directing therapeutic agents specifically to tumor tissues. The mechanisms of action in these systems typically contain the use of nanomaterials to carry and transfer drugs within a control(Luo et al.  2023 ). These nanomaterials are engineered to spot and bind to specific molecular markers expressed on tumor cells. It guarantees that the drug payload is concentrated in the tumor microenvironment. One common mechanism refers to the usage of ligand-receptor interactions. Ligands, like antibodies, peptides, or small molecules, are bind to the surface of nanocarriers(Hennink and Nostrum  2002 ). These ligands specifically interact with overexpressed receptors on the surface of cancer cells. For example, in gynecological cancers, overexpressed folate receptors are observed on the surface of OV cells. Nanocarriers conjugated with folic acid can technically target these cells, facilitating the localized delivery of chemotherapeutic agents (Dodda et al.  2021 ; Hu et al.  2022 ; Porfiryeva et al.  2024 ). Another mechanism used is the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, which takes advantage of the unique properties of tumor blood vessels(Cuenot et al.  2022 ). Tumors have leaky vessels and poor lymphatic drainage, allowing nanoparticles to accumulate more effectively in tumor tissue than in normal tissue. This passive targeting is commonly used for nanoparticle-based drug delivery. Furthermore, stimuli-responsive drug delivery systems release drugs in response to specific tumor microenvironment triggers, such as pH, temperature, or enzyme activity. For example, pH-sensitive hydrogels release drugs in the acidic environment of a tumor, ensuring precise delivery (Han et al.  2020 ). Targeted drug delivery systems offer several significant advantages over traditional chemotherapy. The primary benefit is the reduction in systemic toxicity. Traditional chemotherapy involves the administration of drugs that circulate throughout the body, affecting both cancerous and healthy cells. This non-specific action leads to serious side effects, including hair loss, nausea, and immunosuppression (Lu and Wang  2018 ). In contrast, targeted delivery systems concentrate the drugs at the tumor site, thereby reducing collateral harm on normal tissues. Another advantage is the improved efficacy of the treatment. By delivering more drugs directly to the tumor, these systems can enhance the therapeutic impact while using lower overall doses of the drug. It not only maximizes the drug's efficacy but also mitigates the adverse effects caused by high-dose chemotherapy (Zhu et al.  2024 ; Li et al.  2019 ). Gynecologic‐specific outcomes and implications: In the randomized, open‐label phase III MIRASOL trial (NCT04209855), 453 patients with folate receptor α–positive, platinum‐resistant ovarian cancer received mirvetuximab soravtansine or investigator’s‐choice chemotherapy; mirvetuximab significantly extended median progression‐free survival to 5.62 months (95% CI, 4.34–5.95) versus 3.98 months (95% CI, 2.86–4.47; HR 0.65; P < 0.0001) and median overall survival to 16.46 months (95% CI, 14.46–24.57) versus 12.75 months (95% CI, 10.91–14.36; HR 0.67; P = 0.0046), while reducing rates of grade ≥ 3 adverse events (41.7% vs. 54.1%) and discontinuations due to toxicity (9.2% vs. 15.9%) (Zhu et al.  2024 ; Li et al.  2019 ). Likewise, a retrospective cohort of 69 women with recurrent epithelial ovarian carcinoma treated with extended‐duration single‐agent pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (median 11 cycles, cumulative dose 400 mg/m 2 ) reported a median PFS of 13.0 months (95% CI, 10.7–15.2) and median OS of 40.2 months (95% CI, 30.0–49.0), with a 59.4% clinical‐benefit rate (complete response 17.4%, partial response 13.0%, stable disease 29.0%) and acceptable grade ≥ 3 dermatologic toxicity (31.9%) (Zhu et al.  2024 ; Li et al.  2019 ). These gynecologic‐specific data demonstrate that ligand‐targeted and EPR‐based nanocarriers can deliver both survival gains and improved tolerability in ovarian cancer. Moving forward, optimizing patient selection via FRα expression, refining dosing schedules, and incorporating predictive biomarkers will be crucial to maximize therapeutic index and broaden application to other gynecologic malignancies. Additionally, targeted drug delivery systems can overcome multidrug resistance (MDR) in treating cancer. MDR often results from the overexpression of efflux pumps in cancer cells that expel therapeutic agents, reducing their effectiveness (Xing et al.  2022a ). Nanocarriers can bypass these efflux pumps, ensuring that the drug remains inside the cancer cells long enough to exert its therapeutic effect. The versatility of nanomaterials used in targeted drug delivery also allows for the combination of diagnostic and therapeutic functions. These technologies support simultaneous imaging and therapy of tumors, providing instant feedback on the treatment's progress and allowing for adjustments as needed. Applications in tissue engineering for gynecological cancers Scaffold design and function Scaffolds function in tissue engineering, particularly in the treatment of gynecological cancers, where tissue damage and loss often accompany tumor resection and other therapeutic interventions (Lawrie, et al.  2013a ). The primary function of a scaffold is to provide a three-dimensional structure that supports cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation, promoting functional tissue regeneration. Scaffolds are engineered to mimic the ECM of natural tissues, offering both mechanical support and biological cues necessary for tissue regeneration (Fig.  5 ). This composite illustration delineates the multiscale architecture and mechanotransductive pathways that underlie epithelial integrity and how their dysregulation contributes to tumor progression. In panel a, extracellular matrix fibers (MF) are anchored via integrin–laminin and dystroglycan linkages to the cortical actin cytoskeleton (F-actin), intermediate filaments (IF), and microtubules (MT), transmitting mechanical cues inward to the nuclear lamina and chromatin through the LINC complex and nuclear pore assemblies. The inset highlights focal adhesion clusters and cytoskeletal adaptors that coordinate cell–matrix traction forces. Panel b expands this view to a polarized epithelial sheet, showing how tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions couple neighboring cells to maintain barrier function while interfacing with basal matrix receptors. In cancer, perturbation of these junctional complexes and integrin-mediated adhesions not only weakens tissue cohesion—facilitating invasion through basement membrane remodeling—but also alters nuclear mechanosignaling to drive EMT-associated transcriptional programs. Thus, targeting specific adhesion nodes or restoring normal mechanotransduction offers a promising avenue to impede metastatic dissemination in gynecologic tumors. The ECM-like environment provided by scaffolds helps maintain the phenotypic stability of cells and promotes the deposition of new ECM components, essential for the restoration of tissue architecture and function. This is especially crucial in gynecological cancer patients who may require reconstructive surgery to repair tissue defects following tumor excision. Fig. 5 ( a ) The original model of dynamic reciprocity, representing the minimum required unit for tissue-specific functions, includes the nucleus (N), microtubules (MT), intermediate filaments (IF), microfilaments (MF), and collagen (C). ( b ) A more comprehensive view of dynamic reciprocity The design of scaffolds needs to think about several factors, such as porosity, biodegradability, mechanical strength, and biocompatibility. Porosity is a core indicator that influences nutrient diffusion, cell infiltration, and waste removal within the scaffold (Wang et al.  2022 ). An optimal scaffold should have interconnected pores of appropriate size to facilitate these processes, ensuring that the cells within the scaffold receive adequate nourishment and are able to proliferate effectively. Biodegradability is another key aspect of scaffold design. The scaffold's degradation rate should align with the pace of new tissue formation, ensuring a gradual load transfer to the new tissue without structural failure. Biodegradable polymers, such as PGA, PLA, and their copolymers, are commonly used in scaffold fabrication for their predictable degradation profiles and biocompatibility(Lawrie, et al.  2013b ). Mechanical strength is crucial for scaffolds designed for load-bearing applications, making sure they can tolerate physiological forces without succumbing to collapse or deformation. This is particularly important in gynecological contexts, such as the pelvic floor, which is subjected to significant mechanical stress. Incorporating nanomaterials like carbon nanotubes or graphene can enhance the mechanical properties of scaffolds, providing additional support while maintaining necessary flexibility(Liu, et al.  2021 ). Biocompatibility is equally essential, ensuring the scaffold does not trigger an adverse immune response when implanted(Xu et al.  2020a ). Materials used in scaffold construction should be neither be toxic nor provoke an immune reaction, and promote cellular activities. Natural polymers like collagen, gelatin, and alginate are gradually employed due to their excellent biocompatibility and capability to mimic the natural ECM. Incorporating nanomaterials not only enhances mechanical strength but also allows for the creation of multifunctional scaffolds. These scaffolds can be generated to transfer growth factors or drugs, in direction to the site of tissue repair, enhancing the healing process. For instance, carbon nanotubes and graphene provide structural support and can be functionalized to deliver bioactive molecules, promoting tissue regeneration(Yang et al.  2014 ). Moreover, the flexibility offered by nanomaterials ensures that the scaffold can adapt to the dynamic environment within the body. This adaptability is particularly important in areas subjected to mechanical stress, as it allows the scaffold to support tissue regeneration without compromising its structural integrity (Wang et al.  2022 ). In gynecological cancer treatment, scaffolds can be promoted by growth factors, peptides, and drugs to boost their therapeutic efficacy. For example, scaffolds can be loaded with anti-cancer drugs for localized chemotherapy, which reduces systemic side effects and increases treatment effectiveness(Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Additionally, these scaffolds can be designated to give bioactive agents at a controlled manner, showing a sustained therapeutic effect over time. This approach ensures that the treatment is both targeted and long-lasting, improving patient outcomes. To achieve true customization, hydrogel design should be guided by patient-derived parameters such as tumor molecular profiling (e.g., RNA-seq or proteomic signatures of ER/PR status, growth factor receptors, and matrix-remodeling enzymes) to select optimal bioactive ligands and degradation rates; biomechanical properties measured via shear-wave ultrasound elastography or magnetic resonance elastography to match scaffold stiffness to the patient’s tumor or adjacent stroma; extracellular matrix composition from decellularized tumor biopsies (e.g., collagen I/III ratio and glycosaminoglycan content) to inform polymer choice and crosslink density; protease activity assays (MMP-2/9 levels by zymography or multiplex immunoassay) for selection of enzyme-cleavable linkers; and immune microenvironment metrics (CD8⁺ T-cell and MDSC densities via multiplex immunohistochemistry or spatial transcriptomics) to integrate immunomodulatory cues. Enabling technologies—including next-generation sequencing and mass-spectrometry proteomics for molecular profiling; shear-wave elastography and atomic force microscopy for stiffness mapping; patient-derived organoid cultures for functional validation; 3D bioprinting with CAD/CAM for precise geometry; and microfluidic gradient platforms for spatial patterning—converge to fabricate hydrogel scaffolds that faithfully recapitulate each patient’s tumor biology and mechanics. To ensure clinical success in pelvic‐floor reconstruction, we first establish explicit mechanical benchmarks that any scaffold must meet: Pelvic-floor supports must withstand static compressive stresses up to ~ 15 kPa and peak dynamic pressures of 10–20 kPa (reflecting intra-abdominal pressures of ∼80 mmHg during Valsalva maneuvers) (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Moreover, scaffolds should match the tensile stiffness of native uterosacral ligaments (14.1 ± 1.4 MPa; range 5.7–26.1 MPa) as determined by uniaxial mechanical testing of human cadaveric tissue (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Considering cyclic strains of up to 10% at ∼1 Hz during daily activities, candidate materials must exhibit fatigue resistance beyond 10 5  cycles with < 10% loss of stiffness to avoid mechanical failure in vivo (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Reinforcement strategies—such as incorporation of 3 wt% graphene oxide into polycaprolactone matrices—have demonstrated a fourfold increase in Young’s modulus relative to pure PCL while preserving > 80% elongation at break, confirming the feasibility of achieving the necessary balance of load-bearing capacity and compliance in a dynamic pelvic environment (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Regenerative medicine The usage of hybrid hydrogels in regenerative medicine is particularly beneficial for gynecological applications. For instance, in patients undergoing surgery for ovarian or cervical cancer, there is often a need to repair or reconstruct tissues that have been removed or damaged (Hamoudeh et al.  2008 ). Hybrid hydrogels can be designed to degrade at a controlled rate, allowing them to provide temporary support until the newly regenerated tissue is strong enough to function independently. This degradability is achieved by selecting appropriate biodegradable polymers PLGA and tuning their degradation kinetics to match the tissue regeneration rate (Zhou et al.  2022 ; Ramezani Farani et al.  2022 ). Moreover, hybrid hydrogels can be functionalized with bioactive molecules. These bioactive agents are critical for enhancing the regenerative potential of the hydrogels by promoting cellular activities. For example, the incorporation of VEGF into the hydrogel can stimulate angiogenesis, providing the newly forming tissue with a blood supply necessary for its survival and function (Nigam and Bahadur  2017 ; Hao et al.  2020 ). For clinical translation, hybrid hydrogels have been engineered for minimally invasive implantation and predictable in vivo clearance. They can be delivered through standard 5–12 mm laparoscopic trocars as shear-thinning precursor solutions that rapidly gel in situ under physiological or light-triggered crosslinking, without requiring specialized instruments (Nigam and Bahadur  2017 ; Hao et al.  2020 ). Upon implantation, the hydrogel network supports host cell infiltration and neovascularization, while controlled enzymatic degradation aligns scaffold resorption with new tissue formation over 4–6 weeks. Importantly, incorporating sequential immunomodulatory cues—such as pro-inflammatory solvents that drive early M1 polarization followed by anti-inflammatory moieties that induce M2 polarization—promotes efficient clearance of hydrogel remnants by macrophages and minimizes fibrotic encapsulation (Nigam and Bahadur  2017 ; Hao et al.  2020 ). These materials are ideal for post-surgical repair due to their capacity to degrade at controlled rates, provide temporary structural support, and facilitate tissue regeneration. By incorporating bioactive molecules, these hydrogels can enhance cellular responses and tissue healing, promoting the regeneration of critical tissues damaged by cancer surgery. Their versatility and adaptability position hybrid hydrogels as a powerful tool for improving patient outcomes in gynecological cancer treatment and beyond. Clinical applications The use of hybrid hydrogels in treating gynecological cancer has shown great results in clinical settings. For example, a PEG-based hydrogel loaded with doxorubicin has been tested for ovarian cancer. Clinical trials demonstrated tumor reduction with fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy(Sabbatini et al.  2008 ). The biocompatibility and controlled drug release properties of the hydrogel provided a sustained therapeutic effect, improving patient outcomes. This highlights the potential of hybrid hydrogels as an effective and safer alternative in cancer treatment. Another successful application involves the use of hyaluronic acid-based hydrogels incorporating cisplatin for cervical cancer (Kotcherlakota et al.  2017 ). Clinical trials have indicated that these hydrogels provide localized, sustained release of cisplatin, resulting in improved tumor regression rates and reduced systemic toxicity. The use of hyaluronic acid, showing its natural biocompatibility to interact with cancer cell receptors, has been instrumental in the success of this treatment approach. Recent advancements have also seen the integration of immunotherapy with hybrid hydrogels. For example, a clinical study utilized chitosan-based hydrogels combined with checkpoint inhibitors for treating endometrial cancer (Wang et al.  2020 ). The hydrogel matrix facilitated the localized delivery of immune modulators, boosting the immune response against cancer cells and demonstrating significant improvements in patient survival rates. Thus, hybrid hydrogels have shown great potential in clinical applications for treating gynecological cancer, giving more effective, localized, and safer alternatives to conventional therapies. Their ability to provide controlled drug release, reduce systemic toxicity, and enhance immune responses underscores their promising role in improving patient outcomes and advancing cancer care. Translational Challenges and Clinical Considerations: Bringing hybrid hydrogels from bench to bedside entails navigating complex regulatory pathways for combination drug–device products, often requiring both an Investigational New Drug (IND) application and an Investigational Device Exemption (IDE), as well as compliance with pharmaceutical (e.g., 21 CFR 210/211) and medical-device (21 CFR 820) GMP standards. Achieving batch consistency and scalability demands tight control over polymer molecular-weight distributions, nanomaterial dispersion, and crosslink density—necessitating validated in-process analytics and stringent quality acceptance criteria for each production run. Rigorous safety assessment protocols, aligned with ISO 10993 biocompatibility testing and GLP toxicology studies, must evaluate both acute and chronic responses, including local inflammation, degradation by-products, and systemic exposure associated with long-term implantation. Encouragingly, early-phase clinical trials are now underway: phase I/II studies of thermosensitive poloxamer hydrogels delivering paclitaxel in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, and of hyaluronic acid–cisplatin depots in recurrent cervical carcinoma, have reported acceptable local tolerability and sustained intratumoral retention, though final efficacy data are pending. Addressing these regulatory, manufacturing, and safety hurdles will be essential to realize the full clinical potential of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology.

Scaffold design and function Scaffolds function in tissue engineering, particularly in the treatment of gynecological cancers, where tissue damage and loss often accompany tumor resection and other therapeutic interventions (Lawrie, et al.  2013a ). The primary function of a scaffold is to provide a three-dimensional structure that supports cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation, promoting functional tissue regeneration. Scaffolds are engineered to mimic the ECM of natural tissues, offering both mechanical support and biological cues necessary for tissue regeneration (Fig.  5 ). ( b ) A more comprehensive view of dynamic reciprocity The design of scaffolds needs to think about several factors, such as porosity, biodegradability, mechanical strength, and biocompatibility. Porosity is a core indicator that influences nutrient diffusion, cell infiltration, and waste removal within the scaffold (Wang et al.  2022 ). An optimal scaffold should have interconnected pores of appropriate size to facilitate these processes, ensuring that the cells within the scaffold receive adequate nourishment and are able to proliferate effectively. Biodegradability is another key aspect of scaffold design. The scaffold's degradation rate should align with the pace of new tissue formation, ensuring a gradual load transfer to the new tissue without structural failure. Biodegradable polymers, such as PGA, PLA, and their copolymers, are commonly used in scaffold fabrication for their predictable degradation profiles and biocompatibility(Lawrie, et al.  2013b ). Mechanical strength is crucial for scaffolds designed for load-bearing applications, making sure they can tolerate physiological forces without succumbing to collapse or deformation. This is particularly important in gynecological contexts, such as the pelvic floor, which is subjected to significant mechanical stress. Incorporating nanomaterials like carbon nanotubes or graphene can enhance the mechanical properties of scaffolds, providing additional support while maintaining necessary flexibility(Liu, et al.  2021 ). Biocompatibility is equally essential, ensuring the scaffold does not trigger an adverse immune response when implanted(Xu et al.  2020a ). Materials used in scaffold construction should be neither be toxic nor provoke an immune reaction, and promote cellular activities. Natural polymers like collagen, gelatin, and alginate are gradually employed due to their excellent biocompatibility and capability to mimic the natural ECM. Incorporating nanomaterials not only enhances mechanical strength but also allows for the creation of multifunctional scaffolds. These scaffolds can be generated to transfer growth factors or drugs, in direction to the site of tissue repair, enhancing the healing process. For instance, carbon nanotubes and graphene provide structural support and can be functionalized to deliver bioactive molecules, promoting tissue regeneration(Yang et al.  2014 ). Moreover, the flexibility offered by nanomaterials ensures that the scaffold can adapt to the dynamic environment within the body. This adaptability is particularly important in areas subjected to mechanical stress, as it allows the scaffold to support tissue regeneration without compromising its structural integrity (Wang et al.  2022 ). In gynecological cancer treatment, scaffolds can be promoted by growth factors, peptides, and drugs to boost their therapeutic efficacy. For example, scaffolds can be loaded with anti-cancer drugs for localized chemotherapy, which reduces systemic side effects and increases treatment effectiveness(Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Additionally, these scaffolds can be designated to give bioactive agents at a controlled manner, showing a sustained therapeutic effect over time. This approach ensures that the treatment is both targeted and long-lasting, improving patient outcomes. To achieve true customization, hydrogel design should be guided by patient-derived parameters such as tumor molecular profiling (e.g., RNA-seq or proteomic signatures of ER/PR status, growth factor receptors, and matrix-remodeling enzymes) to select optimal bioactive ligands and degradation rates; biomechanical properties measured via shear-wave ultrasound elastography or magnetic resonance elastography to match scaffold stiffness to the patient’s tumor or adjacent stroma; extracellular matrix composition from decellularized tumor biopsies (e.g., collagen I/III ratio and glycosaminoglycan content) to inform polymer choice and crosslink density; protease activity assays (MMP-2/9 levels by zymography or multiplex immunoassay) for selection of enzyme-cleavable linkers; and immune microenvironment metrics (CD8⁺ T-cell and MDSC densities via multiplex immunohistochemistry or spatial transcriptomics) to integrate immunomodulatory cues. Enabling technologies—including next-generation sequencing and mass-spectrometry proteomics for molecular profiling; shear-wave elastography and atomic force microscopy for stiffness mapping; patient-derived organoid cultures for functional validation; 3D bioprinting with CAD/CAM for precise geometry; and microfluidic gradient platforms for spatial patterning—converge to fabricate hydrogel scaffolds that faithfully recapitulate each patient’s tumor biology and mechanics. To ensure clinical success in pelvic‐floor reconstruction, we first establish explicit mechanical benchmarks that any scaffold must meet: Pelvic-floor supports must withstand static compressive stresses up to ~ 15 kPa and peak dynamic pressures of 10–20 kPa (reflecting intra-abdominal pressures of ∼80 mmHg during Valsalva maneuvers) (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Considering cyclic strains of up to 10% at ∼1 Hz during daily activities, candidate materials must exhibit fatigue resistance beyond 10 5  cycles with < 10% loss of stiffness to avoid mechanical failure in vivo (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ). Reinforcement strategies—such as incorporation of 3 wt% graphene oxide into polycaprolactone matrices—have demonstrated a fourfold increase in Young’s modulus relative to pure PCL while preserving > 80% elongation at break, confirming the feasibility of achieving the necessary balance of load-bearing capacity and compliance in a dynamic pelvic environment (Thulasidasan et al.  2017 ).

Challenges and future directions Current limitations Biologically, the integration of hybrid hydrogels within the human body poses challenges related to biocompatibility and immune response. While these materials are designed to be biocompatible, individual variations in patient responses can lead to unpredictable outcomes. For instance, some patients may experience inflammatory reactions or fibrosis at the site of hydrogel implantation, which can compromise the therapeutic efficacy of the treatment(Bhandari et al.  2022 ). Moreover, the degradation rates of biodegradable hydrogels need to be precisely matched with tissue regeneration rates to avoid premature loss of structural support or prolonged presence of foreign materials, which could lead to chronic inflammation. For immunocompromised gynecologic cancer patients—particularly those recently treated with cytotoxic chemotherapy—may exhibit impaired monocyte/macrophage clearance and dysregulated complement activation upon exposure to nanoparticle–polymer composites. This can result in prolonged hydrogel retention, low-grade inflammation, or hypersensitivity reactions. To mitigate these risks, surface modifications such as PEGylation or zwitterionic coatings are recommended to minimize protein-corona formation; the use of endogenous polymers (e.g., hyaluronic acid or chitosan) can leverage “self” signals to reduce immune recognition; and incorporation of enzyme-degradable linkers (e.g., MMP-cleavable peptides) or low-immunogenic crosslinkers (e.g., genipin) helps ensure controlled clearance without overt activation of host defenses. We further recommend preclinical immunotoxicity screening in chemotherapy-conditioned murine models and in vitro assays using patient-derived PBMCs to fully characterize immune interactions prior to clinical translation. Despite notable advances, several critical challenges hinder the reliable translation of hybrid hydrogels for gynecologic applications. First, reproducibility in hydrogel synthesis remains problematic: minor variations in polymer molecular weight, crosslinking kinetics, or mixing conditions can yield markedly different network architectures and mechanical properties. Second, batch-to-batch variability—driven by inconsistencies in raw-material purity, crosslinker concentration, and processing parameters—often leads to unpredictable drug-loading efficiencies and degradation profiles. Third, sterilization protocols pose a dilemma: common methods such as gamma irradiation, autoclaving, or ethylene-oxide treatment can induce polymer chain scission or alter crosslink density, compromising scaffold integrity and therapeutic payload stability. Finally, in vivo degradation frequently diverges from in vitro expectations due to heterogeneous enzyme activity, localized pH shifts, and variable immune cell infiltration within the pelvic cavity, resulting in inconsistent scaffold resorption and drug-release kinetics. Rigorous process control, standardized quality metrics, validated sterilization methods, and more predictive animal models will be essential to overcoming these hurdles and ensuring reproducible clinical performance. Remaining Gaps and Controversies: Despite remarkable progress in designing and preclinically validating hybrid hydrogels for gynecologic oncology, key gaps and debates persist. First, the mechanistic interplay between specific nanomaterials (e.g., graphene oxide, PLGA nanoparticles) and the complex tumor microenvironment remains poorly defined, with conflicting reports on how hydrogel stiffness and degradation by-products influence ovarian versus cervical cancer cell behaviour. Second, a lack of standardized metrics for mesh size, crosslink density, and rheological properties hinders direct comparison across platforms and laboratories. Third, immunogenicity remains controversial: although genipin-crosslinked chitosan matrices have been reported to elicit minimal inflammation, other studies document macrophage activation and fibrotic encapsulation with similar chemistries. Fourth, the optimal stimuli-responsive trigger (pH, enzyme, thermal, or light) is still debated, as few head-to-head evaluations exist to determine which cue offers the best spatial–temporal control in vivo. Finally, the translational gap is striking—only a handful of formulations have entered early‐phase clinical trials, underscoring challenges in scaling, sterilization, regulatory compliance, and long-term safety. Addressing these controversies through rigorous mechanistic studies, harmonized testing protocols, and coordinated multi-center efforts will be vital to accelerate the clinical translation of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic cancer care. Innovations on the horizon Emerging technologies and materials offer potential solutions to these challenges. One such innovation is developing smart hydrogels which can respond to multiple stimuli, such as pH, temperature, and enzymatic activity. They can provide more controlled and localized drug release, enhancing the precision of cancer treatments(Yu et al.  2022 ). Advanced nanomaterials, including carbon-based nanostructures (graphene and carbon nanotubes) and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), are being explored for their exceptional mechanical properties and functional versatility (Venkatas and Singh  2023 ; Nelson and Bissell  2006 ). These materials can boost the mechanical strength and functional capabilities of hybrid hydrogels, making them more effective in clinical applications. 3D bioprinting technology is advancing the creation of sophisticated and customized hydrogel scaffolds(Varinelli, et al.  2023 ). It allows precise placement of cells, nanomaterials, and bioactive agents within the hydrogel matrix, creating complex tissue constructs that closely mimic natural tissues. This technology could revolutionize hybrid hydrogel fabrication, making them more consistent and scalable for clinical use. By enhancing the precision and scalability of these materials, 3D bioprinting holds the potential to significantly improve the effectiveness and accessibility of hybrid hydrogels in medical applications(Zhou et al.  2021 ). Innovations in gene editing and molecular biology are enhancing hybrid hydrogels. Techniques like CRISPR-Cas9 can modify the genetic makeup of cells within hydrogels, boosting their regenerative capabilities and cancer resistance. Additionally, incorporating engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) into hydrogels improves targeted drug delivery and tissue regeneration. These advancements could significantly improve the effectiveness of hybrid hydrogels in medical applications, making them more adaptable and powerful for various therapeutic uses(Ma et al.  2023 ). Future research needs To fully realize the potential of hybrid hydrogels in gynecological cancer treatment, further investigation is needed in several areas. Comprehensive studies on long-term biocompatibility and biodegradability are vital for safety and efficacy. Research should also optimize the mechanical characteristics of hydrogels to match different tissue requirements, focusing on the effects of nanomaterials and crosslinking methods. Developing standardized fabrication protocols will ensure consistency and reproducibility, facilitating clinical translation. Additionally, clinical trials are necessary to evaluate efficacy, side effects, and patients’ life quality across diverse populations. Although separate lines of investigation have demonstrated the feasibility of targeted drug delivery and tissue regeneration in gynecologic settings, evidence for their concurrent implementation within a single hydrogel platform remains scarce. For instance, folate-conjugated liposomal doxorubicin–loaded hydrogels have been shown to enhance drug accumulation and antitumor efficacy in ovarian cancer models, whereas distinct growth factor–laden hydrogel scaffolds have successfully supported endometrial repair in rodent studies. To date, few reports describe the co-encapsulation of cytotoxic and regenerative cues within the same construct, and their performance in orthotopic gynecologic cancer models has yet to be validated. Bridging these trajectories by engineering dual-payload hydrogels could enable simultaneous eradication of residual malignancy and restoration of normal tissue architecture, representing a promising frontier for multifunctional platform development. Preclinical models for evaluating hybrid hydrogels Preclinical models that most faithfully recapitulate the gynecologic tumor microenvironment include patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) of high-grade serous ovarian and endometrial cancers implanted orthotopically into immunodeficient mice, which preserve native stromal architecture and ECM composition; syngeneic models such as ID8 in C57BL/6 mice, providing an intact immune milieu and peritoneal dissemination; genetically engineered mouse models (e.g., MISIIR-TAg) that develop spontaneous ovarian neoplasms with desmoplastic stroma in an immunocompetent setting; and rapid, cost-effective assays like the chicken chorioallantoic membrane and zebrafish xenografts for early screening of hydrogel biocompatibility, angiogenic potential, and matrix remodeling. By employing this complementary panel, researchers can robustly evaluate in vivo gel rheology, degradation kinetics, controlled release, and downstream effects on vascularization and immune infiltration, thereby streamlining translational development of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology.

Conclusion Hybrid hydrogels show a groundbreaking advancement in the field of biomedical materials, particularly for the treatment of gynecological cancers. These materials combine the beneficial properties of hydrogels, including high water content, biocompatibility, and flexibility—with the enhanced mechanical strength and functional capabilities of nanomaterials. This combination results in versatile platforms that can support targeted tissue engineering, drug delivery, and regenerative medicine. The development of hybrid hydrogels involves various methods of chemical and physical crosslinking, each contributing unique advantages to the final product. Chemical crosslinking provides stability and durability through covalent bonding, while physical crosslinking offers reversible and stimuli-responsive properties through non-covalent interactions. These crosslinking techniques allow for constructing hydrogels with tailored properties suited for specific biomedical applications. In targeted drug delivery systems, hybrid hydrogels enable the precise localization and controlled release of therapeutic agents, minimizing systemic toxicity and enhancing treatment efficacy. Case studies and clinical trials have demonstrated the effectiveness of these systems in improving patient outcomes in gynecological cancer treatment. Moreover, hybrid hydrogels contribute to tissue engineering by offering scaffolds that promote cell adhesion, proliferation, and differentiation, thereby improving tissue regeneration and restoration. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in the production, biocompatibility, and long-term stability of hybrid hydrogels. Addressing these issues through ongoing research and innovation is essential for optimizing their clinical application. Hybrid hydrogels have a significant potential impact on gynecological cancer treatment. They offer a targeted, less toxic alternative to traditional therapies, delivering drugs directly to tumors and reducing side effects, which is especially beneficial for chemotherapy patients. In tissue engineering, hybrid hydrogels enhance reconstructive surgery outcomes, providing better functional and aesthetic results. The future of these materials will be driven by innovations like 3D bioprinting and smart hydrogels. 3D bioprinting allows precise customization for individual patients, while smart hydrogels offer on-demand drug release, improving cancer therapy's effectiveness. Furthermore, interdisciplinary collaboration is essential for advancing the progression of hybrid hydrogels. Material scientists, biomedical engineers, clinicians, and regulatory bodies must work together to solve the problems related to these materials and to establish standardized protocols for their production and use. Such collaboration will indicate that the efficacy of hybrid hydrogels are fully realized in clinical settings. Research going forward should concentrate on improving the mechanical properties and biodegradability of hybrid hydrogels to align with the demands of different tissues. Understanding the long-term biocompatibility and immune responses to these materials is also essential for safety and efficacy. Additionally, exploring the potential of combination therapies involving hybrid hydrogels—such as integrating chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapies within a single platform—could provide synergistic effects and overcome drug resistance. In conclusion, hybrid hydrogels represent a versatile and promising platform for targeted drug delivery and tissue engineering in gynecologic oncology. By combining polymer networks with functional nanomaterials, these systems can achieve controlled degradation, stimuli-responsive release, and mechanical properties tailored to pelvic tissues. Preclinical evidence supports their ability to localize therapeutics and guide regenerative processes with reduced systemic toxicity. Nonetheless, significant translational gaps remain. Standardized, scalable manufacturing under Good Manufacturing Practice conditions must be established to ensure batch‐to‐batch consistency and regulatory compliance. Moreover, robust clinical data from well-powered, randomized phase II/III trials are required to validate safety, immunocompatibility, and efficacy across diverse patient populations. Interdisciplinary collaboration among materials scientists, clinicians, and regulatory bodies will be essential to address these challenges. With rigorous process control and comprehensive clinical evaluation, hybrid hydrogels have the potential to augment current treatment paradigms in gynecological cancer care.
